title: Four Kings for a Conquered Land
subtitle: Indra and Krishna divide Vajranabha's realm among four young princes
story:
The war was over, and now came the harder question: what to do with what the war had won.

In the city of Vajra, where the streets had only just learned to be quiet again, Krishna and Indra moved as conquerors and guests at once. Vajranabha was dead, slain by the discus in Pradyumna's hand; his army was scattered, his allies fled — Nikumbha had gone to ground in the far city of Shatpura. In the streets, boys and old people were still recovering from the fear of the siege; Krishna and Indra had walked among them, consoling them, before turning to the question of the throne. The kingdom lay without a king, and kingdoms do not stay that way for long. So, following the advice of Brihaspati, the wise priest of the gods, Indra and Krishna consulted together about the present and the future.

Their answer was four. It was an answer with a shape: the kingdom would not be absorbed, not abandoned, not given to one conqueror. It would be divided — and divided among the young.

The conquered kingdom was divided into four parts. One fourth went to Vijaya, the son of Indra's son Jayanta, a boy of the divine line who could already range through the upper air. One fourth went to Pradyumna's son. One fourth went to Shamba's son. And the remaining fourth went to Chandraprabha, the son of Gada. Four young princes, each given a realm he had not had to conquer, each carrying a great name on young shoulders. Two houses, one protection: that was the design.

The division did not stop at the throne. The four koti villages of the kingdom were shared out, and a thousand prosperous branch cities like the town of Vajra itself. Warm clothing, deerskins, cloths, and jewels were divided into four parts as well, and Indra and Krishna took pleasure in giving it all away. No one was forgotten in the sharing; the wealth of the dead king became the wealth of the living. There was no grudging in the dividing; it was done openly, generously, in full view of the people.

Then came the crowning. Before the assembled Rishis, Indra and Krishna anointed the four young kings, pouring on their heads the water of the Ganga that issues from Vishnu's feet, while the music of celestial bugles sounded over the city. The Rishis blessed each prince in turn, and the sacred water ran down over the young crowns. Vijaya had already mastered the art of moving through the etherial region; the descendants of Madhava learned it too, inheriting the gift from their mothers, and in time they would travel the sky-road between the celestial region and Dwaraka, the city protected by the Bhaimas.

When the ceremony was done, Indra turned to Jayanta, whose son was among the four. "O heroic victor of armies," he said, "it behoves you to protect all these kings. One of them is a perpetuator of my race; the other three are born in the family of Keshava. By my command none amongst creatures will be able to kill them. Give them elephants born of the quarter-elephants, horses from the race of Ucchaisrava, and chariots built by the celestial architect." And the four kings, newly anointed, bowed and took their places, each in his share of the realm.

And so the city of Vajra, which a season ago had belonged to an asura king, passed into the keeping of four boys. Where one asura king had stood, four young kings now stood. The old king's realm became four realms, held by four young hands — and over them all, one protection, promised by the king of the gods himself.
reflection: The division is not a dispersal: four shares are still one realm under a single protection, and the four young kings receive what they did not have to win. Indra's promise that no creature can kill them is the war, at last, saying it is finished — the children may grow.
next_story_tease: But one member of the great family had still to come home.
